newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian experts see change in World Bank role.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian experts see change in World Bank role.

text.p: The role of the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in development lending is likely to change and Africa should brace itself for this, experts at an economic forum in Nigeria said on Wednesday.
The two multilateral agencies are the main source of funds for development by African nations.

"In the future, the two Bretton Woods institutions may even scale down their role in development lending and be more involved in advising," Kalu Idika Kalu, former Nigerian finance minister and former World Bank economist told the forum.
He said African nations should take advantage of concessionary lending terms by the two agencies and borrow from them now.
"There is an urgent need for African countries to substantially upgrade the level of economic understanding of the two institutions to increase net flow of resources to Africa from them," Kalu added.

The forum was organised by private Nigerian economists to collate ideas for delegates from Nigeria and other African nations to the annual general meeting of the IMF and World Bank to be held in Washington from October 1-3.
The annual meeting attracts ministers and central bank governors from around the world as well as other policy makers.
Ike Abogu, a private consultant told the Lagos forum that the World Bank was poised to work more with the private sector than governments in the future.
"This will be better for Africa," he said, adding that governments in the world's poorest continent had not shown they were capable of managing their economies.
Speaker after speaker said it was time Africa stopped blaming other agencies for its economic woes and tried to evolve correct policies.

"We should be less emotional about the role of the IMF and the World Bank in Africa," said Ade Afolabi, senior manager of the Nigerian Deposit Insurance Coproation, which insures Nigerian banks and has recently been sending many bankers to jail for fraud that has shaken the banking sector.

The IMF and the World Bank have in the past been much criticised for recommending structural adjustment policies for economically troubled African nations that officials say turn out to further impoverish local people.
African nations are reckoned to owe the two agencies about $97 billion, which makes it impossible for some of them to qualify for new loans.
"We have to find a solution to this debt problem and African delegates to Washington should look into this," said Lawrence Ukwu of the conference organisers, Bennen and Tokel.
